CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 18




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                        )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                          )
         FOR AN ORDER OF THE COMMISSION                             )
         APPROVING ITS NEW EXTRA LARGE LOAD                         )
         TARIFF AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF                         )     CASE NO. PUD2026-000046
         SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                               )
         CUSTOMERS AND A REGULATORY ASSET TO                        )
         RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                              )
         PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE                            )

              OG&E’S REPLY IN SUPPORT OF ITS MOTION TO AMEND PROCEDURAL
                SCHEDULE AND ESTABLISH A BRIEFING SCHEDULE REGARDING
                   PROPOSALS FOR ALTERNATIVE SERVICE FRAMEWORKS

                COMES NOW Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “Company”) and

         respectfully submits this Reply in support of its Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule in

         Order No. 758969 to Include a Briefing Schedule Regarding Proposals for Alternative Electric

         Service Frameworks (“Motion”).        The Public Utility Division (“PUD”) and Google LLC

         (“Google”) have filed Responses objecting to the Motion. For the reasons explained below, those

         Responses confirm, rather than refute, the need for focused legal briefing.

                Multiple parties now ask the Commission to require OG&E to offer materially different

         electric-service arrangements involving third-party generation supply, wholesale-market

         transactions, unbundled generation service, capacity accreditation, standby obligations, and

         continued retail delivery by OG&E. These proposals raise substantial and disputed questions

         concerning the Commission’s statutory authority, the Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory

         Act, Oklahoma’s restrictions on retail electric competition, the division between state and federal

         jurisdiction, and the obligations imposed upon regulated public utilities.

                PUD and Google’s Responses devote substantial legal argument to these same questions

         while contending that focused legal briefing is unnecessary. Google expressly recognizes that



         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                        Page 1 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 18




         disputed legal propositions should ultimately be resolved through actual orders and legal briefing

         rather than witness characterization. The dispute is therefore not whether the legal issues require

         consideration, but whether the Commission should address them through an orderly briefing

         process before the Hearing on the Merits or leave them dispersed among witness testimony, pretrial

         motions, hearing argument, and post-hearing proposed findings. The significance of the issues

         warrants the former.

                Good cause exists to amend the procedural schedule to address the legal issues recognized

         by all parties. In addition, no party showed that they would be prejudiced by the addition of legal

         briefing or by a delay of the hearing. OG&E filed the Motion promptly after the disputed proposals

         became part of this Case. The proposed briefing would occur after the completion of all prefiled

         testimony, as OG&E makes no request to change any of the evidentiary filing dates, would allow

         each proponent to defend its own proposal, and would permit the parties to present the Commission

         with a complete legal record before the Hearing on the Merits. The limited adjustment to the

         procedural schedule is reasonable and proportionate to the significance of the issues presented.

         The ALJ and the Commissioners deserve to come into the hearing with the benefit of a fully

         developed factual record and fully briefed legal arguments.

                                                  ARGUMENTS

         A.     PUD and Google’s Responses confirm good cause for focused legal briefing, and
                OG&E’s proposed schedule addresses their timing and record-development
                arguments.

                PUD argues that OG&E lacks good cause because it waited nearly three months after

         learning of a self-supply proposal in Case No. PUD2025-000075. But the parties negotiated and

         presented the schedule to the ALJ on June 24, 2026—before any DODGE stipulation arose in

         either case. The ALJ recommended the schedule on June 25, and the DODGE stipulation was


         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                        Page 2 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 18




         filed June 26. The schedule could not anticipate an unfiled dispute involving another utility.

         Further, any motion for briefing prior to Responsive Testimony would have been premature.

                   Indeed, the dispute only became ripe on September 18, 2026, when primarily PUD and

         Google filed Responsive Testimony proposing to allow large data center customers to dodge

         OG&E’s generation system costs. OG&E moved four days later—before the parties devoted

         further resources to testimony, motions, and hearing preparation.

                   The DODGE proposals independently establish good cause because they raise threshold

         questions concerning the Commission’s authority, certified-territory protections, retail

         competition, state-federal jurisdiction, and OG&E’s public-utility obligations.       PUD’s own

         Response confirms their legal significance by addressing who supplies the customer, whether

         OG&E remains the sole retail supplier, how title passes and transactions settle in the Southwest

         Power Pool, who bears load-serving and resource-adequacy obligations, and what services OG&E

         must provide. Having briefed those issues itself, PUD cannot credibly deny the need for focused

         briefing.

                   Google similarly argues that the existence of disputed legal questions does not establish

         that the Commission cannot hear the evidence and resolve the law under the existing schedule. 1

         That argument frames the issue incorrectly. OG&E does not contend that the Commission lacks

         authority to proceed under the existing schedule. The question is whether that schedule provides

         a fair and orderly mechanism for developing the legal record necessary to decide proposals that

         were not part of OG&E’s Application and were first presented through Responsive Testimony

         approximately six weeks before the currently scheduled Hearing on the Merits.




         1
             Google Response at 2–3.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                        Page 3 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 18




                   Google’s assertion that OG&E identifies no evidence it is unable to present, likewise

        misses the purpose of the Motion. The deficiency is not an inability to introduce evidence. It is

        the absence of an adequate process for counsel to identify, research, and brief the controlling

        statutes, jurisdictional limits, Commission precedent, federal authority, and legal consequences of

        several materially different proposals after the evidentiary positions have been fully developed and

        then the ability to respond to same.

                   PUD also argues that these mixed questions of law and fact “cannot be resolved in the

        abstract before the record is complete.” 2 OG&E requests no such procedure. Briefing would begin

        only after Responsive, Rebuttal, and Sur-Rebuttal Testimony are complete, when the proponents

        will have defined their frameworks, OG&E will have responded, and the proponents will have

        replied. The briefs would therefore address the actual proposals and completed prefiled record,

        not hypothetical arrangements. PUD’s premise thus supports the amendment as the current

        schedule does not permit the parties to complete prefiled testimony, conduct meaningful briefing,

        and prepare for the November 3, 2026 en banc hearing.

                   Google characterizes the requested procedure as a “four-round” briefing sequence that

        should not be made a prerequisite to the Hearing on the Merits. 3 But the sequence follows directly

        from the positions advanced by the objecting parties. PUD insists that the issues cannot be

        resolved before the factual record is complete.       Google separately maintains that technical

        questions should be developed through testimony while disputed legal propositions should be

        resolved through counsel’s arguments and the governing legal authorities. OG&E’s proposed

        schedule does exactly that—it completes the prefiled evidentiary record first, then permits the

        proponents to identify the legal basis for their proposals, provides the other parties an opportunity


        2
            PUD Response at 2.
        3
            Google Response at 1–3.

        OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                         Page 4 of 18
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 18




         to respond, and completes the resulting legal analysis before the Commission convenes the

         Hearing on the Merits.

                Opening briefs are necessary because the proponents request affirmative adoption of

         different frameworks. Responses are necessary because those frameworks would alter OG&E’s

         legal and service obligations. Replies permit each proponent to answer the objections to its own

         proposal. A limited sur-reply prevents new legal arguments or authorities raised in reply from

         escaping meaningful response. The sequence is neither excessive nor duplicative given the number

         of proponents, the differences among their proposals, and the significance of the legal questions

         presented.

                The Commission’s decision must ultimately be based on substantial evidence and must

         comply with state statutes. The Commission must determine the scope of its statutory authority,

         compliance with certified-territory protections, whether the arrangements constitute unauthorized

         retail wheeling or third-party retail service, whether OG&E may be compelled to facilitate third-

         party generation supply, and consistency with Oklahoma’s regulatory structure. Those questions

         must be resolved before or as part of any order imposing DODGE. Focused, responsive briefing—

         not legal conclusions dispersed through unqualified witness testimony, hearing argument, or post-

         hearing findings—is the orderly means to resolve them and provide the Commission an adequate

         legal record.

         B.     The PSO proceeding demonstrates that the legal record was underdeveloped and
                reinforces the need for a complete record in this case.
                PUD argues that OG&E’s discussion of Case No. PUD2025-000075 is inaccurate and

         irrelevant because OG&E had an opportunity to address the DODGE issues through two filings




         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                      Page 5 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 18




         submitted as public comment in that proceeding. 4 That argument ignores both the procedural

         posture of OG&E’s filings and the limited legal record upon which the ALJ’s recommendation was

         based. Far from making additional briefing unnecessary, the PSO proceeding demonstrates why

         the Commission should require a complete legal record before deciding whether to consider a

         similar framework in this Case.

                   In Case No. PUD2025-000075, a non-unanimous stipulation, from the PUD and large data

         center interests, asked the Commission to adopt a DODGE framework opposed by PSO. PSO

         argued that the proposed framework constituted unauthorized retail wheeling, conflicted with the

         Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act, and exceeded the Commission’s statutory

         authority. Although the ALJ ultimately recommended approval of the disputed framework, the

         ALJ’s Report resolves the disputed statutory and jurisdictional questions in only a few paragraphs. 5

                   This is not a criticism of the ALJ, who resolved a single issue within the broader general

         rate case based on the record presented and the limited procedural posture and time remaining after

         the unexpected DODGE stipulation. But the Report was issued without an orderly process for

         opening, response, and reply briefs addressing the controlling statutes, the Commission’s authority,

         certified-territory protections, retail wheeling, and the interaction between state-regulated retail

         service and federally regulated wholesale transactions.              Its abbreviated treatment of those

         substantial legal issues therefore cannot substitute for a fully developed record here—particularly

         when PUD asks the Commission to import the same general framework into this Case, adapt it to

         OG&E’s system, and defer material implementation details to a later compliance filing.




         4
             PUD Response at 3, 9.
         5
             Report and Recommendation of the Administrative Law Judge, Case No. PUD2025-000075, at 9–13.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                                 Page 6 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 18




                 The PSO stipulation itself also disclaims precedential effect in other proceedings. 6

         Moreover, the ALJ’s Report is only a recommendation to the Commission—the Commission has

         not yet issued a Final Order approving the stipulated framework or resolving the disputed legal

         issues. The legality of the proposals in this Case therefore cannot be presumed merely because an

         ALJ recommended approval of a different framework, applicable to a different utility, on a

         different and procedurally limited record.              Nor can PUD rely upon OG&E’s constrained

         participation as a nonparty in that proceeding as a basis to deny OG&E and the other parties a

         meaningful opportunity to brief the legal issues now squarely presented here.

                 Further, if the Commission adopts any DODGE proposal in this Case, the resulting order

         will present significant questions for appellate review. The Commission and any reviewing court

         should have the benefit of a record—in this Case—in which the relevant statutes, competing

         interpretations, jurisdictional arguments, and legal authorities have been fully developed by the

         parties. Focused briefing will assist the Commission in making adequate findings and conclusions,

         protect the integrity of its decision, and facilitate meaningful judicial review. Avoiding the

         development of that record does not promote judicial economy. It merely postpones the legal

         dispute until after the Commission has acted.

         C.      Witness testimony and existing procedural mechanisms are not an adequate
                 substitute for legal briefing.
                 PUD argues that OG&E can adequately address the disputed issues through Rebuttal

         Testimony, Sur-Rebuttal Testimony, pretrial motions, oral argument, and Proposed Findings of




         6
           Google now acknowledges the same point. Google does not contend that the proposed stipulation or the ALJ’s
         recommendation in the PSO proceeding binds the Commission in this Case and does not assert that a Final Order
         approved the disputed stipulation. Google Response at 3; Google Response to Motion to Strike at 4–5. That concession
         confirms that the Commission cannot treat the PSO proceeding as having resolved the legal issues now presented here.
         See also Joint Stipulation and Settlement Agreement, Case No. PUD2025-000075, § 12.5.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                                      Page 7 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 18




        Fact and Conclusions of Law. 7 Those procedures serve different purposes and do not replace

        focused legal briefing.

                Rebuttal and Sur-Rebuttal Testimony are evidentiary filings.              They permit qualified

        witnesses to present facts and expert opinions within their respective fields of expertise. They are

        not the proper vehicle for counsel to brief statutory interpretation, Commission jurisdiction, the

        legal effect of judicial and administrative authority, or the division between state and federal

        jurisdiction.

                The problem is not theoretical. OG&E separately filed its Motion to Strike Portions of the

        Responsive Testimony of Google witness Adrian J. Kimbrough, or alternatively to disregard the

        challenged testimony in resolving legal issues. Mr. Kimbrough expressly acknowledges that he is

        not an attorney, but then offers conclusions concerning the meaning of Oklahoma statutes, the

        Commission’s legal authority, the Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act, retail wheeling,

        and erroneously, “direct and binding administrative precedent.” 8

                Google’s Response to OG&E’s Motion to Strike reinforces the need for focused legal

        briefing. Google expressly states that it does not ask the Commission to treat a witness’s assertion

        that self-supply is lawful, or that another proceeding supplies “direct and binding” precedent, as

        dispositive proof of Oklahoma law. Google further acknowledges that the status and legal effect

        of the PSO proceeding should be resolved from “the actual orders and legal briefing, not witness

        characterization.” 9 That concession substantially narrows the procedural dispute. Google agrees

        that witness testimony does not resolve the controlling legal questions and that legal briefing is the

        proper mechanism for determining the effect of the governing authorities.



        7
          PUD Response at 5.
        8
          See Kimbrough Responsive Testimony 52:6–53:22; OG&E’s Motion to Strike, Entry No. 43.
        9
          Google Response to Motion to Strike at 4–5.

        OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                             Page 8 of 18
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 18




                OG&E does not challenge the ability of qualified economic, financial, engineering, or

         ratemaking witnesses to testify concerning matters within their expertise.         But a witness’s

         discussion of tariff design, cost allocation, market settlements, or operational mechanics cannot

         substitute for legal advocacy concerning whether the Commission possesses statutory authority to

         order the proposed arrangement. Those disputed legal questions should be addressed by counsel

         through briefing that identifies and analyzes the applicable statutes, constitutional provisions,

         judicial decisions, Commission rules, Commission orders, and federal authority.

                Nor are pretrial motions, oral argument, or Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of

         Law adequate substitutes for a general briefing schedule. Pretrial motions typically seek specific

         relief, such as excluding testimony or resolving a discrete procedural issue—they do not provide

         every party an orderly opportunity to present and answer affirmative legal arguments concerning

         each proposed service framework. Oral argument likewise cannot develop legal authorities as

         systematically as written briefs. And because Proposed Findings and Conclusions are submitted

         only after the Hearing, they come too late to inform the presentation of evidence, the treatment of

         testimony offering legal conclusions, or the Commission’s consideration of those issues during the

         Hearing.

                PUD and Google cannot persuasively contend that these questions must be considered on

         a developed factual record, acknowledge that witness characterization does not resolve disputed

         propositions of law, and nevertheless insist that focused legal briefing is unnecessary. The parties

         substantially agree on the proper division of responsibility: witnesses should develop the technical

         record, counsel should brief the law, and the Commission should decide both on a complete record.

         OG&E’s proposed schedule provides the orderly means to accomplish that result.




         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                         Page 9 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 18




         D.         The proposed briefing sequence does not shift OG&E’ burden of proof on the
                    Application to intervenors.
                    PUD argues that the proposed schedule improperly shifts OG&E’s burden of proof because

         proponents of DODGE would file opening briefs and OG&E would have the opportunity to file

         responsive and sur-reply briefs. 10      That argument confuses OG&E’s burden to support its

         Application with the Intervenors’ obligation to support their separate affirmative relief.

                    OG&E accepts its burden as the Applicant to establish that its proposed XLPL Tariff and

         related Terms and Conditions are fair, just, reasonable, and consistent with Oklahoma law. OG&E

         filed Direct Testimony and supporting exhibits for that purpose. OG&E’s burden does not,

         however, require the Company to anticipate and disprove in its direct case DODGE proposal that

         an intervenor might later propose. Nor does OG&E’s status as the Applicant relieve parties seeking

         affirmative Commission adoption of those DODGE frameworks from having the burden of

         supporting their own counter recommendations.

                    PUD and the intervenors are not merely opposing a provision of OG&E’s proposed tariff.

         They ask the Commission to require OG&E to offer service options that OG&E did not request,

         to unbundle components of retail service, to facilitate third-party generation arrangements, and to

         assume continuing delivery and reliability obligations. Parties requesting that affirmative relief

         should identify the legal authority they contend permits the Commission to grant it. Requiring a

         party to defend the legality of the relief it affirmatively requests does not transfer OG&E’s burden

         as the Applicant. It recognizes the ordinary and reasonable principle that a party proposing a

         materially different framework must support that proposal.

                    The order of briefing is likewise procedural. It does not determine the ultimate burden of

         persuasion. The proponents file first because only the proponents can definitively identify the


         10
              PUD Response at 7.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                         Page 10 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 18




         precise framework they request and the legal authority upon which they rely. OG&E and other

         parties may then respond to those arguments. The proponents may reply, and parties may address

         new arguments raised in reply.

                    PUD’s preferred alternative would produce the true inequity. Under PUD’s theory, an

         intervenor could request affirmative adoption of a materially different service framework without

         first identifying the legal basis for the proposal, while OG&E would bear the obligation to prove

         that the unrequested framework is unlawful. Nothing about OG&E’s Applicant status requires that

         result.

         E.         No party has demonstrated any prejudice and the proposed schedule is proportionate,
                    nonprejudicial, and procedurally fair.
                    PUD characterizes the proposed schedule amendment as a ten-week delay that would

         impose tangible costs and require parties with materially different positions to jointly defend a

         composite framework that none of them proposed. 11 Neither contention establishes prejudice or

         justifies denying OG&E’s request for focused legal briefing.

                    The Motion leaves unchanged the existing deadlines for Rebuttal Testimony, the settlement

         conference, Sur-Rebuttal Testimony, and discovery. 12 The proposed amendment therefore does

         not postpone development of the prefiled evidentiary record, interfere with ongoing discovery, or

         prevent the parties from continuing settlement discussions. It adjusts only the subsequent pretrial

         and hearing-related dates so that the parties may brief the threshold legal issues after all prefiled

         testimony has been submitted.

                    PUD identifies no evidentiary right that would be lost, no party whose ability to present its

         case would be impaired, and no specific pending transaction that would be jeopardized by the



         11
              Id. at 6, 8–9.
         12
              OG&E’s Motion at ¶ 10.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                           Page 11 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 18




         proposed schedule. Although the Hearing on the Merits would move approximately ten weeks,

         that period is limited when measured against the nature and potential consequences of the relief

         requested by PUD.

                    The DODGE proposals could substantially alter the structure of regulated retail electric

         service in Oklahoma. The proposals resemble a form of electric restructuring that Oklahoma

         considered, but did not implement, following the California energy crisis and the market abuses

         exposed during the Enron era. Taking approximately ten additional weeks to ensure that the

         Commission has a complete legal record before deciding questions of that magnitude is neither

         unreasonable nor disproportionate. The Commission should not accelerate a decision affecting

         Oklahoma’s longstanding regulatory compact—a compact that has resulted in some of the lowest

         rates in the country—merely to preserve a schedule developed before these questions were raised.

                    PUD also asserts that the requested adjustment would leave prospective customers without

         the protections of an approved large-load tariff. 13 But PUD identifies no transaction conditioned

         upon entry of an order by the existing hearing date, no concrete commercial decision that would

         be affected by the requested adjustment, and no prospective large-load customer that would

         otherwise be subject to the XLPL tariff to begin taking service before a Final Order would be

         entered under the amended schedule.

                    Google’s reliance on Case No. PUD2026-000031 affirmatively demonstrates the absence

         of customer harm. That proceeding concerns separately negotiated Electric Service Agreements

         governing service to Google’s three data-center projects. If approved, those agreements will

         govern the non-rate terms and conditions under which Google receives service. Google therefore

         will not be subject to the Terms and Conditions of XLPL Service, regardless of whether the



         13
              PUD Response at 8.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                       Page 12 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 18




         Commission issues a Final Order in this Case in November 2026 or approximately ten weeks later.

         Google’s ability to proceed with its projects, receive electric service, and obtain the protections of

         its negotiated agreements will not be affected by the requested schedule amendment.

                Nor will the requested amendment affect the rates Google pays. Under the Electric Service

         Agreements, Google will initially be billed under the LPL-TOU tariff. Although the agreements

         permit the Commission to migrate Google to an applicable large-load tariff, the initial rates

         proposed for XLPL service are tied to the existing LPL rates. Those rates are not expected to

         diverge until the Commission establishes cost-based XLPL rates in OG&E’s next general rate case,

         after XLPL customers have begun taking service and the costs attributable to the new class can be

         studied.   Thus, whether the Commission approves the XLPL Tariff in November 2026 or

         approximately ten weeks later will not change the rates Google pays during that period. Google’s

         invocation of Case No. PUD2026-000031 therefore proves the opposite of what Google suggests:

         the Commission can take the limited additional time necessary to develop a complete legal record

         without delaying Google’s projects, altering its contractual protections, or increasing its rates.

                Nor will the proposed amendment impair ongoing commercial discussions involving other

         prospective large-load customers. Neither PUD nor Google identifies any prospective customer

         expected to begin taking service under the XLPL Tariff during the approximately ten-week period

         at issue, any commercial decision contingent upon the existing Hearing date, or any rate

         consequence resulting from the proposed amendment. Their generalized appeals to timing and

         regulatory certainty do not establish actual prejudice.

                Proceeding without adequate briefing, by contrast, carries substantial legal and regulatory

         risk. An order adopting a DODGE framework without a complete legal record could create




         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                         Page 13 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 18




         substantial regulatory uncertainty. A limited schedule adjustment now reduces the risk of greater

         uncertainty, additional litigation, and avoidable appellate issues later.

                    Google also notes that OG&E’s proposed Hearing date would fall after the publicly stated

         end of Commissioner J. Todd Hiett’s current term. Although Google disclaims any allegation that

         OG&E selected the proposed dates to obtain a particular Commissioner or outcome, Google

         nevertheless invites the ALJ and Commission to assign significance to that timing. 14 The

         insinuation is unsupported and should play no role in resolving this procedural Motion as OG&E

         maintains no control over Commission terms and their timing.

                    OG&E’s proposed dates follow directly from the existing testimony deadlines and the time

         required for the requested briefing sequence. More fundamentally, this Case is pending before the

         Oklahoma Corporation Commission as an institution, not before any individual Commissioner.

         The need for a complete legal record does not change based upon which Commissioners may

         ultimately participate in the Hearing or Final Order. If the Commission determines that different

         individual dates would better accommodate its calendar while preserving meaningful briefing,

         OG&E has already indicated its willingness to accept reasonable scheduling adjustments. The

         identity of a potential decision-maker, however, is not a legitimate reason to deny the Commission

         a complete legal record.

                    PUD further argues that the proposed briefing deadlines would burden the parties because

         they fall near Thanksgiving and the year-end holidays. 15 OG&E specifically considered the

         holiday calendar when developing its proposed schedule and selected filing dates intended to avoid

         anticipated holiday conflicts. PUD identifies no actual scheduling conflict or specific inability to

         comply with the proposed deadlines. Its generalized concern therefore does not establish prejudice


         14
              Google Response at 4.
         15
              PUD Response at 8.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                       Page 14 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 18




         or justify denying briefing altogether. If an unforeseen conflict arises, the ALJ/Commission may

         reasonably adjust an individual filing date while preserving the essential briefing sequence.

                     PUD’s separate contention that the proposed schedule would require all “DODGE

         Proponents” to file a single brief defending a composite framework also misconstrues the

         Motion. 16 Under OG&E’s proposal, each party seeking adoption of a DODGE framework may

         file a separate brief-in-chief supporting its specific proposal and requested relief. PUD would

         defend its proposal, and Google would defend its own; no party would be required to join another’s

         brief, reconcile competing frameworks, or defend a proposal it did not advance. Any party may

         respond, each proponent may reply in support of its proposal, and any party may file a limited sur-

         reply addressing new matters raised in reply. This sequence gives every party a fair opportunity

         to be heard on each distinct proposal.

                     Allowing separate opening briefs will narrow rather than blur the disputed issues. Each

         proponent will be required to identify the precise arrangement it asks the Commission to approve.

         Responsive briefing will then permit parties to address each specific framework and the legal

         theories advanced in support of it. The process will also allow the Commission to distinguish

         among the proposals rather than treating all alternative service arrangements as legally or

         operationally identical.

                     The proposed schedule is therefore proportionate and procedurally fair. It preserves the

         existing testimony, discovery, and settlement deadlines; causes no identified commercial or

         customer harm; accommodates the holiday calendar; permits each proponent to defend its own

         proposal; and provides the focused legal briefing that Google itself recognizes is necessary to

         distinguish technical evidence from disputed propositions of law. The limited adjustment is



         16
              Id. at 6.

         OG&E’s Reply in Support of Motion for Briefing                                        Page 15 of 18
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 57 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/30/2026 - PAGE 16 OF 18




         justified by the gravity of the legal questions presented and will materially assist the Commission

         in resolving those questions on a complete and orderly record.

                                              REQUESTED RELIEF

                WHEREFORE, OG&E respectfully requests that the Commission establish, a formal legal

         briefing schedule and modify the dates set forth in Order No. 758969 substantially as requested in

         the Motion. In the alternative, if the Administrative Law Judge or Commission determines that
